title: MathCursor — Getting started
intro: For each instruction, try it in the box on the right. Type, look, repeat. Spaces mean something in MathCursor: they separate what's grouped. Every example in this document is checked automatically against the engine: what you read is exactly what you'll get.

sections.title: How the popup works
sections.intro: As soon as MathCursor recognizes a notation, a small window appears above the cursor with the main conversion (preselected) and the possible alternatives. `Enter` accepts the selected suggestion. `Down arrow` then `Enter` picks an alternative. `Esc` closes the popup and pauses automatic detection for this document: handy when you write a document without math (history, literature…). `Ctrl + Space` resumes detection and forces the popup to appear; a second `Ctrl + Space` extends the zone leftward.

sections.title: Fractions
sections.intro: Type the `/` operator. The space decides where the fraction stops.

items.instruction: With a space, the fraction stops before the `+`. Type `1/x +1`.
Glued, MathCursor keeps the standard reading but offers the extension as an alternative. Type `1/x+1`.
Spaces around the `/` group each side. Type `x+1 / x+2`.

sections.title: Powers and subscripts
sections.intro: A digit glued to a letter makes a POWER: `x2` gives x². For a SUBSCRIPT, type `_`: `u_n`. Word's Subscript and Superscript buttons work too while typing: type `f`, click Subscript, type `2+1`, you get f₂₊₁.

items.instruction: Type `x2`: the power inserts directly, with no alternative to choose.
`U_n+1` is ambiguous: the popup offers U_{n+1} as an alternative.

sections.title: Greek letters
sections.intro: Write their name in full. The CAPITAL of the first letter picks the uppercase Greek letter: `pi` gives π, `Pi` gives Π. Letters inserted from Word's Symbol menu (λ, Δ…) are understood too.
sections.note: If the popup doesn't appear on its own, `Ctrl+Space` opens it.

items.instruction: Glued, it untangles. The area of a disk: `pir2`, the popup lets you choose between πr² and (πr)².

sections.title: Roots and functions
sections.intro: Functions are written as words: `sqrt`, `cos`, `sin`, `ln`… Glued or spaced, both work: `cosx` ≡ `cos x`.

items.instruction: `cos x+1` glued: the popup offers to extend the argument.
Exponential: `e^x` or `exp(x)` give the same thing. Type `e^x`.

sections.title: Vectors and geometry
sections.intro: `vec` adds the arrow, glued (`vecAB`) or spaced. Uppercase point pairs are understood: lines `(AB)`, segments `[AB]`, parallel `//`, perpendicular `perp`.

items.instruction: Type `vec AB`: wide arrow over both letters.
Angle: `angle ABC` (or the shortcut `^ABC`) adds the wide hat.

sections.title: Sets and logic
sections.intro: English words work: `in`, `forall`, `exists`, `union`, `inter`, `subset`. Number sets are chosen in the popup (R variable or ℝ set).

items.instruction: Type `x in R`: the popup offers the double-struck ℝ version.

sections.title: Intervals
sections.intro: Brackets + semicolon: `[a;b]`. Open brackets work both ways.

sections.title: Sequences and limits
sections.intro: `lim` takes the variable, the bound, then the expression, separated by spaces. `inf` is infinity.

items.instruction: With a sequence: `lim n inf u_n = 0`.

sections.title: Sums, integrals, counting
sections.intro: `sum` takes the index, the bounds, then the expression. `int` takes the bounds, the expression, the variable.

items.instruction: Same logic for the n-th root: `root 3 8`.

sections.title: Complex numbers
sections.intro: `conj` adds the conjugation bar, `abs` the single bars, glued or spaced.

items.instruction: All glued untangles: `rexp(itheta)`, that is r, exponential, i and theta.

sections.title: Physics: units and scientific notation
sections.intro: The decimal comma is understood as well as the point. A unit after a number is set in roman type. For powers of 10, type `10` followed directly by the exponent: the popup offers scientific notation.

items.instruction: Negative exponent: `1*10-4` gives 1×10⁻⁴. The “minus 4” reading stays as an alternative.
Positive exponent: `3*108 m/s`, pick 3×10⁸ in the popup.
The micro prefix (inserted from the Symbol menu): `T=20µs`.

sections.title: Matrices
sections.intro: Inside parentheses: a comma OR a space separates columns, the semicolon separates rows.

items.instruction: Type `(a,b,c;d,e,f)`: a 2×3 matrix. With spaces, `(a b c; d e f)`, same result.

sections.title: Symbols and LaTeX input
sections.intro: `+-` gives ±. If you know LaTeX, your habits work: `\sum`, `\forall`, `\leq`, `infty`… with or without the backslash. Symbols pasted from a problem statement (≤, √, x⁻¹, H₂O…) are understood too.

sections.title: The popup, your ally
sections.intro: When several readings are equally valid, MathCursor offers them ALL, and it's consistent: if you repeat the same pattern, it reads it the same way on both sides.

items.instruction: `(a,b,c)`: as is (tuple), row or column? The popup lets you choose.

sections.title: Chaining a calculation
sections.intro: On the same line: convert `f(x)`, then type `=2` right after it. MathCursor merges both into a single formula f(x)=2. Over several lines: go to a new line and start with `=` or `<=>`. The new line aligns under the previous one, in the same equation block, which you can keep extending line after line.
